title: A function and its derivative on one shared axis: where is it steep, flat or singular?
summary: Two stacked panels with the same x axis: the function above, its derivative below. Zeros of the derivative line up with the flat spots of the function, and numerical check dots show the derivative was verified.

media.alt: Top panel: a smooth teal curve f(x) with four marked flat points. Bottom panel: its derivative as a dashed curve with orange check circles lying on it, crossing zero at the same x as the flat points.
media.caption: Reference render of class F1.2 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: Where is it steep, flat, singular?
read_the_figure.axes: Shared x for both panels, 0 to about 12.6. Top y: f(x). Bottom y: f'(x), with a red zero line. The panels have different vertical scales on purpose.
look_at: Follow each dotted vertical line from the bottom panel to the top: where f' crosses zero, f has a peak or a trough.
Where is f' largest in size? That is the steepest part of f (the annotation 'steepest' at x = 0, f' = 1.1).
Do the check circles sit on the dashed analytic curve? Agreement at sampled points verifies the derivative formula.
Which way does f' cross zero? Down through zero: a maximum of f. Up through zero: a minimum.
as_drawn: Four flat points at x = 1.57, 4.41, 8.00 and 10.49, marked with amber squares on f and dotted lines through both panels.
The check dots are central differences at 13 points; they lie on the analytic curve to the eye.
Both panels share x exactly, so vertical lines compare one x in both. Their y scales differ, so the height of f' must not be compared with the height of f.
read_the_figure.proves: That the derivative formula and the function are consistent at the checked points, and that the flat spots are where f' changes sign. It does not prove agreement between the dots, and it says nothing about places with no dots.
if_wrong: Panels with different x ranges: vertical lines lie.
Derivative drawn alone, with no numerical check: a sign error in the formula would go unnoticed.
A derivative that is spiky or jumps while f looks smooth: noise amplification, or a kink in f.

terms.meaning: The slope of the tangent line: how fast f changes per unit x.
A point where f' = 0. It may be a maximum, a minimum or an inflection with zero slope.
An estimate of f' from two neighbours, one each side: (f(x+h) - f(x-h)) / 2h.
The spacing h used in a finite difference. Too large: truncation error. Too small: round-off.
Panels stacked so that equal x positions line up vertically.
A point where f or f' is infinite or undefined, such as a vertical tangent or a jump.

remember: Zeros of f' sit under peaks and troughs of f.
f' > 0: f rising. f' < 0: f falling. |f'| large: steep.
Shared x axis, always; different y scales are fine but must be labelled.
A numerical check (dots) turns a formula into a verified formula.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position on x is shared. Position on y encodes f in the top panel and f' below. The solid teal line is the function, the dashed sky line the analytic derivative, open amber circles the numerical estimate, squares the critical points, the red horizontal line is f' = 0. Dotted vertical lines tie the panels together.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A derivative is a local, hidden property of the curve: the slope. Plotting it as its own curve makes it a quantity you can read directly, and putting it under the function lets the eye link cause and effect: f' crosses zero exactly under each flat spot, and f rises while f' is positive.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: The vertical scales of the two panels are independent, so a derivative curve that looks larger than the function does not mean the function changes faster than it is. Derivatives amplify noise: a function that looks smooth can have a very noisy derivative. And agreement at 13 dots says nothing about the points in between.

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: A shared x axis makes the vertical guide lines honest. Numerical-check dots catch algebra mistakes (sign, factor) because two independent routes to f' must agree. Without them a clean-looking derivative curve is only a claim.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Overlay both on one axis only when they have comparable size. For classification of critical points, add f'' as a third panel. For a quick feel for steepness, draw tangent segments on f. For noisy data, differentiate a smoothed fit, not the raw points.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a third panel with f'' and colour the stretches where f is concave up and down. Replace central differences with complex-step or automatic differentiation and show the error of each on a log axis.

steps.title: Central difference and its error
steps.note: Halving h cuts the error by four. For this f at x = 2 the error is 9.6e-4 at h = 0.1, 9.6e-6 at h = 0.01 and 9.6e-8 at h = 0.001: a factor 100 per decade of h, as the h-squared law predicts.

steps.title: Classifying a flat point from f' alone
steps.note: In the render the crossings at 1.57 and 8.00 go from plus to minus (maxima); 4.41 and 10.49 go from minus to plus (minima).

steps.title: The steepest point
steps.note: At x = 0 the derivative is 1.1, and |f'| never exceeds that on [0, 4 pi], matching the 'steepest' label.

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure: (1) at which x does f first become flat and is that a maximum or a minimum? (2) What is the steepest slope? (3) Do the check dots confirm the analytic derivative?

solution.text: The first dotted line is at x about 1.57. There f' crosses zero going downward, so f has a maximum, at height about 0.98 in the top panel.
f' is largest at the left edge, where the annotation says steepest: f'(0) = 1.1. The function climbs from 0 to about 0.98 in the first 1.57 units.
The circles lie on the dashed curve at all 13 points; the error at h = 0.001 is about 1e-7, far below the width of a line.

worked.answer: First flat point x = 1.57, a maximum; steepest slope 1.1 at x = 0; the numerical check agrees with the formula at the sampled points.

analyze.q: A numerical-check dot lies clearly off the analytic curve at one x. List two possible causes.
analyze.hint: A wrong formula, a wrong h, or a feature narrower than h.

analyze.q: Why do the vertical dotted lines matter more than the shape of the lower curve?
analyze.hint: They link the two panels at identical x.

analyze.q: What would the bottom panel look like if f had a corner? Sketch it.

evaluate.q: Is agreement at 13 sample points enough to call a derivative verified? What else would you test?
evaluate.hint: Check near the ends, near sharp features, and with a different h.

create: Add a third panel with f'' and mark inflection points where f'' changes sign.
Redraw with noise added to f and show what central differences do at h = 0.01; then smooth first.

checks.q: What does it mean for the f' panel to cross zero while f is at its peak?
checks.hint: Think of a tangent line at the top of a hill.
checks.answer: The tangent is horizontal at a peak, so the slope is zero. A peak is a down-going zero crossing of f'.

checks.q: A central difference with h = 0.1 has an error of 1e-3. What h gives about 1e-5?
checks.answer: h = 0.01: one tenth of h gives one hundredth of the error, 1e-5.

checks.q: The check dots agree perfectly but a colleague says the plot proves nothing. Are they right?
checks.hint: What could go wrong that the dots cannot see?
checks.answer: Partly. The dots verify the formula where they sit. They cannot see behaviour between them, at singular points, or at other h, so they are necessary evidence, not complete proof.
